newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS sees shift to "exotic" currencies.
newsitem.headline: BIS sees shift to "exotic" currencies.

text.p: Trade in "exotic" currencies is growing as volatility and margins shrink in established foreign exchange markets, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said in its annual report.
European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), calling in its third stage for phasing in a single European currency, the Euro starting in 1999, will reduce volume further.
An estimated 10 percent of the current foreign exchange market could be lost with introduction of the single European currency, BIS said.
EMU "holds out the prospect of declining activity in a market already adjusting to narrower spreads," it said.
Global foreign exchange market turnover averaged $1.19 trillion a day based on an April 1995 survey by central banks and monetary authorities in 26 countries.

The BIS meanwhile estimated daily currency volume at $1.572 trillion on an average daily basis, including some international double counting to permit analysis of the impact of introduction of the Euro.
Trade in European Union currencies, estimated by BIS at $1.099 trillion daily in April 1995, shrank to $799 billion if adjustments for monetary union were factored in.
"Faced with these challenges, foreign exchange dealers are focusing on the growth of trading in currencies from outside the industrial countries," BIS said.
"Data from official and market sources suggest that trading in currencies not captured by the 1995 survey is expanding rapidly," BIS said.
The next survey, to be done in 1998, will be expanded to more than the 26 countries, it said.
It said the aggregate volume of such business already "has reached over one-third of the volume in the intra-European trading that may disappear with the introduction of the Euro."
Volume in the Indonesian rupiah versus dollar and yen for example was about the same as volume in lira traded versus the mark in April 1995.
Trade in currencies in newly emerging foreign exchange markets also offered wider spreads, an attractive feature given the narrowing of bid/offer spreads in conventional markets.
BIS noted that spreads narrowed partly a result of introduction of increased electronic trading.

Two big electronic foreign exchange dealing systems, one called the Electronic Broking Service (EBS) and run by a consortium of banks, and another sold by Reuters Plc, have also led to a further erosion of spreads.
"In the past 18 months the volume traded over the EBS (and over Reuters as well, although volume figures are not available) has expanded very rapidly," BIS said.

"Once a given currency pair attains critical mass, electronic broking can offer very narrow spreads, of one or two hundredths of a pfennig in dollar/mark trading, for example, which is about one-third of previous spreads," BIS said.
